q: During crystallisation, the hot saturated solution is filtered before it is left to cool. The purpose of this filtration is to:
o: Remove insoluble impurities
Remove soluble impurities
Make larger crystals form
Dry the crystals
x: Insoluble impurities stay on the filter paper while the dissolved compound passes through; soluble impurities stay in the mother liquor after cooling. Thinking this step removes soluble impurities is the common slip.

q: A crude solid is being purified by crystallisation, but its hot solution is coloured by an impurity. The colour is best removed by:
o: Adding more solvent and cooling quickly
Washing the final crystals with hot solvent
Boiling the solution with a little animal charcoal and filtering it hot
Heating the crystals until the colour disappears
x: Animal charcoal adsorbs coloured impurities and is removed by hot filtration, leaving a colourless solution to crystallise. Washing with hot solvent would dissolve the product itself, and heating the crystals does not remove the impurity.

q: A mixture contains iodine, sand and sodium chloride. Which sequence separates all three?
o: Add water and filter; heat the filtrate to sublime the iodine; the residue is sand
Add water and evaporate; sublime the residue to get the salt; the sand stays behind
Heat gently to sublime the iodine; add water to the residue and filter off the sand; evaporate the filtrate to get the salt
Heat strongly to melt the salt; filter off the sand; cool to get iodine crystals
x: Iodine sublimes, so it is removed first by gentle heating; sand is insoluble and salt is soluble, so water and filtration separate them, and evaporation gives the salt. Adding water first dissolves some iodine with the salt, and NaCl does not sublime or melt at a practical temperature.

q: Iodine is extracted from its aqueous solution by shaking it with carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄ (density 1.59 g cm⁻³), in a separating funnel. After the layers settle, the iodine is mainly in the:
o: Upper layer, which is violet
Lower layer, which stays colourless
Upper layer, which stays colourless
Lower layer, which is violet
x: CCl₄ is denser than water (1.0 g cm⁻³) and immiscible with it, so it forms the lower layer; non-polar I₂ dissolves far better in CCl₄, giving a violet colour. Taking the organic layer always to be on top (true for ether, not CCl₄) gives the upper-layer answer.

q: In fractional distillation of a mixture of ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water, a fractionating column is fitted because it:
o: Gives a large surface on which vapour condenses and re-evaporates many times, so the vapour reaching the top is rich in ethanol
Cools the vapour so that both liquids condense together
Stops the water from boiling at all
Raises the boiling point of ethanol above that of water
x: Each condensation and re-evaporation on the column's packing enriches the vapour in the more volatile ethanol, so it separates two miscible liquids whose boiling points are not far apart. The column does not stop water boiling or change the boiling points.

q: For a compound X, (concentration in ether) ÷ (concentration in water) = 2 at equilibrium. 9.0 g of X is dissolved in 100 cm³ of water and extracted with two successive 50 cm³ portions of ether. The total mass of X extracted into the ether is:
x: With 50 cm³ ether: (mₑ/50) ÷ (m_w/100) = 2, so mₑ = m_w and each portion takes half of what is left: 4.5 g, then 2.25 g, total 6.75 g. One 100 cm³ portion would take only 6.00 g, and stopping after the first portion gives 4.50 g.

q: In paper chromatography, the stationary phase is:
o: The solvent that rises up the paper
Water held in the cellulose fibres of the paper
The mixture applied as a spot
The vapour of the solvent in the jar
x: The paper's fibres hold a film of water, which is the stationary phase; the solvent moving up the paper is the mobile phase. Mixing up the stationary and mobile phases is the usual slip.

q: When a paper chromatogram is set up, the base line carrying the spots must be above the level of the solvent in the jar. Otherwise:
o: The solvent would not rise up the paper at all
The spots would dissolve into the solvent in the jar instead of moving up the paper
The Rf values of all spots would become 1
The spots would move faster and give larger Rf values
x: If the spots dip into the solvent, the substances wash out into the solvent in the jar and no chromatogram forms. The solvent still rises by capillary action whatever its level.

q: A mixture gives two spots on a paper chromatogram, 2.0 cm and 5.0 cm from the base line, when the solvent front has moved 8.0 cm. In the same solvent, pure substances have Rf values P 0.25, Q 0.40, R 0.625 and S 0.75. The mixture contains:
o: P and R
Q and S
P and S
Q and R
x: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front: 2.0/8.0 = 0.25 (P) and 5.0/8.0 = 0.625 (R). Measuring the spots from the solvent front instead of the base line gives 0.75 and 0.375, pointing wrongly to S and Q.

q: To dilute concentrated sulphuric acid safely, you should:
o: Add the water slowly to the acid
Add the water quickly to the acid
Warm the acid first and then add the water
Add the acid slowly to the water, stirring all the time
x: Mixing gives out a lot of heat; adding acid to a large volume of water lets the water absorb the heat. Adding water to the acid can make it boil locally and spit concentrated acid.

q: A salt solution is acidified with dilute HCl and then BaCl₂ solution is added. A white precipitate forms that does not dissolve in the acid. The anion present is:
o: CO₃²⁻
Cl⁻
NO₃⁻
SO₄²⁻
x: BaSO₄ is a white precipitate insoluble in dilute HCl. BaCO₃ would dissolve in the acid with effervescence (and the acid removes carbonate first), while chloride and nitrate give no precipitate with Ba²⁺.

q: 0.53 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate is dissolved in water and titrated with 0.10 mol dm⁻³ HCl using methyl orange: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. The volume of acid needed is: (C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23)
o: 50 cm³
200 cm³
100 cm³
10 cm³
x: Na₂CO₃ = 106 g mol⁻¹, so 0.53 g = 0.005 mol; HCl needed = 2 × 0.005 = 0.010 mol; volume = 0.010/0.10 = 0.100 dm³ = 100 cm³. Forgetting the 1 : 2 ratio gives 50 cm³.
